gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for a four-HDD RAID 5 pool on a NAS in this price class: PCWorld measured 430 MB/s read and 340 MB/s write over the DXP4800 GT's 10GbE port with four WD Red Plus drives. One 2.5GbE port carries about 295 MB/s (half of QNAP's lab figure for two ports), so 10GbE only pays off with an SSD or NVMe pool behind it. The UGREEN boxes have M.2 slots for that pool; the QNAP TS-432X has none and needs a QM2 card in its only PCIe slot.
standout_why: I compared against our own page, which gives an unsourced estimate of 'roughly 400–600 MB/s' for HDD RAID 5 and no measurement. ChooseCompute's 4-bay guide only says 'over 1,000 MB/s' for the Plus and never covers HDDs against 10GbE. QNAP's TS-432X page, cited by ChatGPT, gives 1,181 MB/s, but only with four SATA SSDs. Every ChatGPT answer says 'four HDDs in RAID 5 often won't saturate 10GbE' or gives an unsourced '400–700 MB/s'. None names a measurement, says that HDD writes (340 MB/s) are only about 15% faster than one 2.5GbE port, or ties the fix to the M.2 lanes. ChatGPT does show 'NVMe slots 0' for the TS-432X but doesn't explain what that means for 10GbE. I did not open itechguides, starryhope, kuibu or computingforgeeks, which were not cited.
decides: This supports the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus and DXP4800 GT over the QNAP TS-432X for this shopper. With hard drives only, any of the three runs at roughly 340–430 MB/s, so the 10GbE port barely matters. To use the port fully you need an SSD or NVMe pool. The UGREENs have two M.2 slots built in: on the GT they run at PCIe 3.0 x2, and NAS Compares got 1.45 GB/s read in RAID 0, which is more than 10GbE carries. The TS-432X needs SATA SSDs in its drive bays (QNAP's own 1,181 MB/s test) or a QM2 card in its single PCIe Gen3 x4 slot. Both cost extra and the bay route gives up HDD capacity. The finding doesn't separate the Plus from the GT: both get about 9.4 Gbit/s on the wire.

findings.label: Measured RAID 5 HDD throughput over 10GbE (large video files)
findings.source_title: Ugreen DXP4800 GT review: This Ryzen NAS makes 10GbE affordable (PCWorld, Christoph Hoffmann and Michael Rupp, 2026-09-22)
findings.note: Four 2 TB WD Red Plus drives in RAID 5. The client was a Windows PC with a 10GbE card, connected through a switch with Cat 7 cable. The same review measured 65 MB/s with 20,000 small files and about 780 MB/s combined with two clients.

findings.label: iperf3 network-only throughput and 10GbE controller
findings.value: 9.4 Gbit/s; Aquantia AQC113 controller on the two 10GbE ports
findings.note: 9.4 Gbit/s is about 1,175 MB/s. Against that link, the 430 MB/s HDD read above uses about 37% of it.

findings.label: Maker's lab SMB sequential throughput, 1× 10GbE and 2× 2.5GbE
findings.value: 10GbE: 1,181 MB/s read, 887 MB/s write. 2× 2.5GbE: 590 MB/s read, 590 MB/s write
findings.note: QNAP's test conditions: '4 x Samsung 860 PRO 512GB, RAID 5, thick volume', QTS 5.1.7.2743, IOmeter 16MB sequential. These are SSDs, not HDDs. 590 / 2 ports ≈ 295 MB/s for one 2.5GbE port, which I used as the 2.5GbE ceiling. 340 MB/s HDD write ÷ 295 ≈ 1.15×.

findings.label: NVMe path
findings.value: No M.2 slots; one PCIe Gen 3 x4 slot
findings.note: The hardware spec lists 'Slot 1: PCIe Gen 3 x4' and no M.2. The product page (https://www.qnap.com/en-us/product/ts-432x) says the QM2-2P-344A card can 'Add two M.2 SSDs to create a storage pool or enable SSD caching' (host interface PCIe Gen3x4). That uses the only slot.

findings.label: 10GbE port type
findings.note: The spec page does not list which transceivers or DACs are supported. The product page lists the TRX-10GITSFPP-SR (850 nm SR optical) as an optional accessory.

findings.label: M.2 lane width and measured NVMe pool speed
findings.value: PCIe Gen 3 x2 per M.2 slot; 2× NVMe RAID 0 just above 1.45 GB/s read, about 1.1 GB/s write
findings.source_title: UGREEN DXP4800GT NAS Review (NAS Compares, Rob Andrews, 2026-06-08)
findings.note: Rob Andrews calls these 'storage testing' and does not say they were measured over the network. Four SATA SSDs gave about 1.3 GB/s read and 600–700 MB/s write. He did not test U.2.

findings.label: UGREEN's own statement on HDD RAID 5 vs 10GbE
findings.value: Four NAS HDDs in RAID 5 'generally deliver around 600 to 700 MB/s under favorable sequential conditions'; 10GbE 'theoretical ceiling of 1.25 GB/s'
findings.source_title: Best UGREEN 4-Bay NAS: Compare Current Models (UGREEN)
findings.note: This is the maker's claim and is higher than PCWorld's measured 430/340 MB/s. The same page says of the GT: 'Two 10GbE ports do not turn one ordinary file transfer into a 20Gbps connection... A single TCP session remains limited by one link.'
